w10_P4_001796: A calibration sheet at a roller-coaster launch bay lists two candidate speed readings, in meters per second, for a test cart: the two numbers add up to 13 and multiply together to give 40. Records confirm the true reading is the smaller of the two. Multiplying that speed by 8 gives the actual launch speed of a cart with a mass of 58,000 grams. Find the energy this cart carries at that speed, in joules, then multiply that number by 5. Convert what results into kilojoules. What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001797: The final number a crane-hoist engineer records, in kilonewtons, is obtained by multiplying an earlier figure by 10, and then by 8 more. Before those multiplications, the value was a kilonewton reading converted from a force in newtons that a 61 kilogram hoist arm exerts while undergoing a certain acceleration. That acceleration, in meters per second squared, is how sharply the arm's motion is changing at t = 2 seconds, given that its position, in meters, follows s(t) = 2t^3 + 5t^2 for t in seconds since the motor engages. (The hoist cable is rated for 6 metric tons, a fact that plays no role here.) What is the final number, in kilonewtons?
w10_P4_001798: The final number a drone-rotor test lab records, in kilojoules, is 10 less than an earlier figure, which is itself 4 less than a kilojoule reading converted from an energy value in joules. That joule value is the energy a 17,000 gram rotor blade carries while moving at a speed that is 21 more than the number of different ways a technician could choose 4 blades out of 6 identical spares on the shelf. What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001802: The final number a wind-turbine nacelle test crew logs, in kilojoules, is obtained by multiplying a converted energy figure by 5, after that figure was already multiplied by 9. Before that, the value was the energy, in joules, carried by a 7 kilogram test mass moving at a speed that is 19 more than the speed gained by a component between t = 1 second and t = 2 seconds, given that the component's acceleration, in meters per second squared, follows a(t) = t^2 + 4t over that interval. What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001803: The final number an escalator-motor engineer reports, in kilonewtons, comes from converting a force value that is 24 more than an earlier newton reading. That earlier reading is the push a 194,000 gram gearbox exerts while accelerating at a rate that is 21 less than a value obtained by multiplying an earlier reading by 10. That earlier reading, in meters per second squared, is the smaller of two candidate accelerations on a calibration sheet: two numbers that add up to 11 and multiply together to give 28. (The escalator handrail moves at 0.5 meters per second, a fact that plays no role here.) What is the final number, in kilonewtons?
w10_P4_001810: The final number a flywheel test lab logs, in kilojoules, is 6 less than an earlier figure, which is itself 16 more than a value that was, before that, 2 less than a kilojoule reading converted from an energy value in joules. That joule value is the energy a 6 kilogram flywheel segment carries while moving at a speed equal to the larger of two candidate readings on the calibration sheet -- two numbers that add up to 15 and multiply together to give 56. (The flywheel housing spins inside a chamber holding 3 liters of lubricant, a detail with no bearing on the numbers here.) What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001814: The final number a hydraulic-press bench technician records, in kilojoules, is obtained by multiplying an earlier figure by 5. That figure is itself 24 less than a kilojoule reading converted from an energy value, in joules, carried by an 18 kilogram ram head moving at a certain speed. That speed, in meters per second, is how fast the ram is moving at t = 1 second, given that its position, in meters, follows s(t) = 3t^3 + 5t^2 for t in seconds after the stroke begins. (The press frame stands 2.4 meters tall, a fact that plays no role here.) What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001828: The final number a car-engine test rig reports, in kilojoules, comes from converting an energy value that had first been multiplied by 7. That unmultiplied energy, in joules, is what a 46,000 gram piston assembly carries while moving at a speed that is 3 less than the larger of two candidate readings on a calibration sheet -- two numbers that add up to 7 and multiply together to give 12. What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001829: At a piston test cylinder, a piston's position, in meters, follows s(t) = 5t^3 - 2t^2, where t is the time in seconds after ignition. Engineers need the piston's speed at t = 2 seconds. That speed applies to a piston with a mass of 18,000 grams. Find the energy this piston carries at that speed, in joules, then multiply that number by 5, then add 8, and then add 6 more. What is the final number, in joules?
w10_P4_001831: The final number a wind turbine nacelle test crew logs, in kilojoules, comes from converting an energy value that had already been multiplied by 3, after being reduced by 10 and increased by 14. Before those adjustments, the value was the energy, in joules, carried by a 58,000 gram calibration mass moving at a speed equal to the greatest length, in centimeters, that divides evenly into both a 195 centimeter cable and a 77 centimeter cable with nothing left over. What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001838: The final number a forklift test yard crew records, in kilonewtons, is obtained by multiplying an earlier figure by 8. That figure is itself 26 less than a kilonewton reading converted from a force in newtons that a 124 kilogram test load exerts while accelerating at a rate equal to the number of different groups of 3 pallets a technician could choose from 6 identical pallets on the yard. (The forklift's mast reaches 4.5 meters high, a fact that plays no role here.) What is the final number, in kilonewtons?
w10_P4_001843: The final number a skateboard-ramp test lab logs, in kilojoules, is obtained by multiplying a converted energy reading by 8. That reading, in joules before conversion, is the energy a 57 kilogram rider model carries while moving at a speed that is 25 more than the smaller of two candidate readings on a calibration sheet -- two numbers that add up to 8 and multiply together to give 15. (The ramp's guard rail is painted with 2 liters of sealant, a detail that plays no role here.) What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001846: The final number a magnetic-rail-launcher engineer records, in kilojoules, is obtained by multiplying an earlier figure by 8, after that figure was already multiplied by 12 and by 9. Before those multiplications, the value was a kilojoule reading converted from an energy value, in joules, carried by a 27,000 gram sled moving at a speed gained between t = 3 seconds and t = 4 seconds, given that the sled's acceleration, in meters per second squared, follows a(t) = 4t^2 + 6t over that interval. What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001849: At a catapult test rig, technicians run 5 successive launch cycles. On cycle k (for k = 1 through 5), the arm adds exactly 2k minus 1 extra units of tension beyond its base setting; adding up the extra tension from all 5 cycles gives a total, which becomes the acceleration, in meters per second squared, of a counterweight with a mass of 87,000 grams. Find the push this counterweight requires, in newtons, then add 2 to that number, then multiply what remains by 11, and then by 6. Convert the result into kilonewtons. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?
w10_P4_001852: At a robotic-arm joint test bench, a joint's position, in meters, follows s(t) = t^3 + 3t^2, where t is the time in seconds after actuation. Engineers need the joint's speed at t = 2 seconds. That speed acts as the acceleration, in meters per second squared, of a housing with a mass of 134 kilograms. (The housing's mounting plate is 0.7 meters across, a fact that plays no role here.) Find the push this housing requires, in newtons, then convert that number into kilonewtons. Multiply the result by 6, then by 8, and then add 1 more. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?
w10_P4_001853: At a crane hoist facility, two support cables measure 325 centimeters and 209 centimeters. Technicians want the greatest length, in centimeters, that divides evenly into both cables with nothing left over, and that length becomes the acceleration, in meters per second squared, of a counterweight with a mass of 194,000 grams. Find the push this counterweight requires, in newtons, then multiply that number by 10, then by 6, then add 3, and then multiply the result by 6. What is the final number, in newtons?
w10_P4_001854: The final number a pinball-launcher test rig reports, in kilonewtons, is obtained by multiplying an earlier figure by 2. That figure is itself 18 more than a kilonewton reading converted from a force in newtons that an 84 kilogram plunger head exerts while accelerating at a rate equal to the total acceleration gained between t = 3 seconds and t = 4 seconds, given that the rate at which the plunger's acceleration builds up -- its jerk, in meters per second cubed -- follows j(t) = 4t^2 + 4t over that interval. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?
w10_P4_001860: At a go-kart track test bay, a kart's position along the straightaway, in meters, follows s(t) = t^3 + 2t^2, where t is the time in seconds since the start. Engineers need the kart's speed at t = 2 seconds. That speed applies to a scale-model kart with a mass of 28 kilograms. Find the energy this kart carries at that speed, in joules, then convert that number into kilojoules. Subtract 10 from the result, then multiply what remains by 10, and then by 7. What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001861: The final number a piston test cylinder crew logs, in kilonewtons, comes from converting a force value in newtons that is 7 more than an earlier figure, which is itself 28 more than a force reading a 62 kilogram piston assembly exerts while undergoing a certain acceleration. That acceleration, in meters per second squared, comes from a bench test repeated 4 times, where each repetition combines a baseline push worth 2 units with an extra push worth 2 units, and adding together the results from all 4 repetitions. (The cylinder head bolts are torqued to 45 newton-meters, a detail that plays no role here.) What is the final number, in kilonewtons?
w10_P4_001862: The final number a forklift test yard crew reports, in kilonewtons, comes from converting a force value in newtons that had first been multiplied by 12, then by 2. The unmultiplied force is what a 147 kilogram test load exerts while accelerating at a rate equal to the speed a linkage reaches at t = 1 second, given that its position, in meters, follows s(t) = 5t^3 - 3t^2 for t in seconds after actuation. (The forklift's tires are inflated to 90 psi, a fact that plays no role here.) What is the final number, in kilonewtons?
w10_P4_001873: A calibration sheet at a conveyor-belt test bench lists two candidate acceleration readings, in meters per second squared, for a gearbox housing: the two numbers add up to 10 and multiply together to give 21. The correct reading is the larger of the two. That acceleration acts on a housing with a mass of 93,000 grams. Find the push this housing requires, in newtons, then add 4 to that number, then subtract 6, and then subtract 28 more. What is the final number, in newtons?
w10_P4_001876: The final number a robotics-lab technician logs, in joules, is 9 less than an earlier figure, which is itself 13 less than an energy reading that had been multiplied by 10. The unmultiplied energy, in joules, is what a 43 kilogram test arm carries while moving at a speed equal to the number of different groups of 3 servo motors a technician could choose from 8 identical units on the shelf. What is the final number, in joules?
w10_P4_001884: The final number a robotics-lab technician records, in kilojoules, is 15 more than an earlier figure that had been multiplied by 2. That earlier figure came from converting an energy value, in joules, carried by a 46 kilogram test arm moving at a speed equal to the number of different pairs a technician could choose from 10 identical sensors on a shelf. (The shelf itself is 1.8 meters long, a detail that plays no role here.) What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001885: At a robotic-arm joint test bench, a joint's position, in meters, follows s(t) = t^3 + 4t^2, where t is the time in seconds after actuation. Engineers need the joint's acceleration at t = 4 seconds. That acceleration acts on a housing with a mass of 163,000 grams. Find the push this housing requires, in newtons, then multiply that number by 5. Convert what results into kilonewtons, and then subtract 2 more. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?
w10_P4_001886: At a water pump station, technicians run 10 successive test cycles. On cycle k (for k = 1 through 10), the pump adds exactly k extra liters per minute to its base flow rate; adding up the extra flow from all 10 cycles gives a total, which becomes the speed, in meters per second, of a 36 kilogram test slug in the pipe. Find the energy this slug carries at that speed, in joules, then subtract 25 from that number. Convert what remains into kilojoules, subtract 23 more, and then multiply the result by 11. What is the final number, in kilojoules?
